items.stem: Should voters have to show a photo ID to vote?
options: No; signature checks and other methods are enough
Yes, but accept many kinds of ID, give IDs free, and allow a backup option for people without one
Yes, a government-issued photo ID, with no backup option

items.stem: Should people have to show a document proving citizenship, like a passport or birth certificate, when registering to vote?
items.scope: Today people swear they are citizens, under penalty of law.
options: No; the sworn statement and existing checks are enough
Only when government records can't confirm citizenship
Yes, everyone registering must show such a document

items.stem: Who should be able to vote by mail?
options: Every voter, with ballots mailed automatically
Any voter who asks
Only voters with a reason, like illness or travel
Almost no one; vote in person

items.stem: Should mail ballots that arrive after Election Day count if they were mailed by Election Day?
items.scope: Ballots with a postmark on or before Election Day.
options: Yes, if they arrive within a week or more
Yes, if they arrive within 3 days
No; only ballots received by Election Day

items.stem: Should eligible citizens be registered to vote automatically when they deal with government agencies, like getting a driver's license?
items.scope: Only people the agency confirms are eligible citizens.
options: Yes, unless they choose to opt out
Offer registration, but people must choose to sign up
No; people should register on their own

items.stem: When should people convicted of a felony be able to vote?
options: Always, even while in prison
Once released from prison
After finishing parole or probation
Only after a waiting period or an individual review
Never

items.stem: How should the president be elected?
items.scope: This would apply to elections from now on, whichever party it might help.
options: By national popular vote, ending the Electoral College
Keep the Electoral College, but divide each state's votes in proportion to how the state voted
Keep the Electoral College as it is

items.stem: Is it acceptable for a candidate to win the presidency while getting fewer votes nationwide than the opponent?
items.scope: This has happened 5 times, most recently in 2016.
options: No; it should be impossible
Acceptable, but the system should change to make it rarer
Yes; it reflects the role of states in choosing the president

facts.claim: Popular-vote loser won the presidency in 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016

items.stem: Who should draw the lines for congressional districts?
items.scope: Answer whichever party it might help in your state.
options: Independent commissions with no politicians involved
Commissions with equal members from both parties
State legislatures, once every 10 years after the census
State legislatures, whenever they choose, including mid-decade

items.stem: Should there be limits on how much corporations, unions and wealthy individuals can spend on elections?
items.scope: Spending on ads and campaigns, not direct donations to candidates.
options: Yes, strict limits, with a constitutional amendment if needed
No limits, but full disclosure of who pays for political ads
No limits or disclosure rules; spending on politics is free speech

items.stem: Should candidates get public money for their campaigns if they agree to spending limits?
options: Yes, matching small donations several times over
Yes, a modest amount
No public money for campaigns

items.stem: Should members of Congress have term limits?
items.scope: Limits on total years served in each chamber.
options: Yes, 12 years or less
Yes, about 18 to 24 years
No; voters can remove them
items.notes: Popular across parties; may load on POP rather than VOTING.

items.stem: Should Supreme Court justices serve a fixed term instead of for life?
options: Yes, 18 years
Yes, but longer, around 25 years
No; keep life terms
